lead: When Yeshua calls His disciples ‘little children’ and also prays to the Father, both the Father’s self-revelation in the One who came as a man and Yeshua’s genuine prayer and obedience from the human position are brought into view.

blocks.text: Biblical quotations in this article are based on the King James Version (KJV). In accordance with the terminology used throughout this article, ‘Jesus’ in the KJV is rendered as ‘Yeshua.’ Greek terms are followed by their Romanized pronunciation.

When reading the New Testament, we encounter an important distinction between the way Yeshua addresses His disciples and the way He prays to the Father. If this distinction is understood simply as meaning that the Father and the Son are two separate Gods, it becomes difficult to fully explain the meaning of the incarnation—that God came as a man.
In John 13:33, Yeshua addresses His disciples as ‘little children.’
Little children, yet a little while I am with you. Ye shall seek me: and as I said unto the Jews, Whither I go, ye cannot come; so now I say to you.

The Greek word translated as ‘little children’ is τεκνία (teknia). Its singular form, τεκνίον (teknion), is a diminutive of τέκνον (teknon, child). Literally, it can mean ‘little children,’ while in context it can also carry the affectionate sense of ‘dear children.’ It therefore functions less as a reference to the actual age of those being addressed and more as a relational term of affection, such as that used by a parent or teacher toward those regarded as children.

Yeshua was about thirty years old when He began His public ministry, while Scripture does not state the exact ages of His disciples. Nevertheless, in John 13, τεκνία (teknia) is clearly addressed to adult disciples. Therefore, the expression should not be understood merely in terms of physical age.

The important question here is who is speaking from within Yeshua. Yeshua tells Philip that to see Him is to see the Father, and He also states that the words He speaks are not spoken from Himself, but that the Father dwelling in Him performs His works.
Yeshua saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? He that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Shew us the Father?
Believest thou not that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? The words that I speak unto you I speak not of myself: but the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works.

Therefore, when Yeshua speaks to His disciples, we should not look only at the visible human body before them. The Gospel of John itself explains that the Father speaks and works in Yeshua, who is present in human flesh. From this perspective, the expression ‘little children’ need not be read merely as an ordinary age-related expression spoken by a man in His thirties to other adults. It may be understood as a relational address in which the Father, manifested in the man Yeshua, speaks to those who are His children.
Yet at this point an even more difficult question arises. The same Yeshua also prays to the Father. In Gethsemane, Yeshua prays:
And he said, Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee; take away this cup from me: nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt.
The Greek text reads Ἀββᾶ ὁ πατήρ (Abba ho pater), meaning ‘Abba, Father.’ Likewise, in John 17:1, Yeshua lifts His eyes toward heaven and addresses Πάτερ (Pater), ‘Father.’

If this scene is considered by itself, the Son and the Father can appear to be two completely separate beings. This naturally raises the question: ‘If Yeshua is God, is God praying to Himself?’ Such a question becomes even more difficult when the incarnation is understood merely as God temporarily assuming the outward appearance of a human being.
Scripture first says this concerning God:
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.

God is Spirit in His essential mode of existence. Yet when God revealed Himself among humanity, He truly entered human life. He did not merely appear to be human. He entered the human condition, experiencing hunger, weariness, sorrow, tears, suffering, prayer, obedience, and even death.
The Epistle to the Hebrews expresses this point very clearly:
Who in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, and was heard in that he feared.

The Greek text describes this as ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ (en tais hemerais tes sarkos autou), literally, ‘in the days of His flesh.’ The prayer was something Yeshua actually offered while He was ‘in the flesh.’ Therefore, describing this merely as God speaking to Himself does not adequately explain the reality of the incarnation.

Since Yeshua came as a man, He truly took the position of humanity. As a man, He depended upon the Father. As a man, He obeyed. As a man, He suffered. As a man, He prayed. He did not merely assume the human position outwardly while exempting Himself from it because He was God. He stood in the place of humanity, sought the Father, and submitted Himself to the Father’s will.

At precisely this point, we must consider together both ‘the Father speaking in Yeshua’ and ‘Yeshua praying to the Father.’ The former reveals the self-revelation of the Father dwelling in Yeshua, who is seen as a man. The latter reveals the genuine human obedience of Yeshua, who humbled Himself to the place of humanity.

This, therefore, is not merely a form of self-conversation. Within the event of God becoming man, the relationship is revealed between the invisible God, who is Spirit, and Yeshua, who truly took flesh and stood in the place of humanity. The One who took flesh did not regard the flesh itself as the divine essence. Rather, standing in the human position, He sought the Father and submitted Himself to the Father’s will.
Yet this does not make Yeshua and the Father two different Gods. Yeshua states clearly:
I and my Father are one.

He also says, ‘He that hath seen me hath seen the Father,’ and declares that the Father dwells in Him. Therefore, the distinctions revealed in Scripture should not immediately be interpreted as a separation within God. At the same time, the unity of God should not be used to erase the real distinction and genuine prayer revealed in the incarnation.

The point to be emphasized is this. God the Father is Spirit, and that God revealed Himself among humanity. Yeshua, who was visible to human eyes, was truly human, yet at the same time the Father spoke and worked in Him. For this reason, Yeshua could say, ‘He that hath seen me hath seen the Father,’ and He could address His disciples as ‘little children,’ speaking to them as one speaks to one’s own children.

At the same time, Yeshua, who came as a man, prayed to the Father from the position of humanity. His prayer was not merely a formal scene in which God prayed to Himself. Rather, it revealed how completely God humbled Himself to the human condition. The One who came as a man depended upon the Father and obeyed Him from within the human position, while remaining one with the Father who dwelt in Him.

Therefore, Yeshua cannot be fully understood through a simple either-or question: ‘Is He the Father, or is He the Son?’ Scripture shows the Father speaking in Yeshua while also showing Yeshua, in the flesh, praying to the Father. A distinction is present, but that distinction does not mean a division of God. Yeshua, revealed in human form, is the self-revelation of God the Father to humanity, while His prayer and obedience show how completely God humbled Himself to the place of humanity.
